extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, philosophers of science, and researchers evaluating hypotheses and explanations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for forming, using, and testing scientific hypotheses and for deciding when a law is explanatory (derivative) or ultimate. Emphasizes the interplay of deduction and induction and limits of reductionist explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: “An hypothesis is any supposition which we make (either without actual evidence, or on evidence avowedly insufficient) in order to endeavor to deduce from it conclusions in accordance with facts which are known to be real; under the idea that if the conclusions to which the hypothesis leads are known truths, the hypothesis itself either must be, or at least is likely to be, true.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses may relate to causes or modes of production and, if admitted, will serve to explain facts deducible from them. Examples: (a) cause real but law supposed (e.g. various suppositions about planetary force prior to inverse-square law); (b) fictitious cause but supposed to act by laws similar to known phenomena (e.g. Descartes' vortices vs. vibratory ether).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that hypotheses be testable by legitimate induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To entitle an hypothesis to be received as one of the truths of nature ... it must be capable of being tested by the canons of legitimate induction, and must actually have been submitted to that test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification by specific experience is indispensable. An hypothesis may be a useful technical aid initially, but to be accepted as true it must be tested and verified by experiment/observation rather than left untested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of hypotheses: to explain by deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the hypothesis relates to the cause or mode of production of a phenomenon, it will serve, if admitted, to explain such facts as are found capable of being deduced from it. Explaining, in the scientific sense, means resolving a uniformity which is not a law of causation into the laws of causation from which it results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypotheses to deduce known regularities and thereby convert empirical generalizations into causal explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and analogy as constraints on hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses that 'ally themselves by analogy with known laws of nature' possess plausibility; purely arbitrary suppositions lacking such analogy are unlikely to be persuasive or useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hypotheses that connect with known phenomena/laws. Avoid inventions that posit both a fictitious agent and a fictitious law without grounding (anti-pattern: wholly fictitious agents with arbitrary laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to base deductive reasoning on experimentally established premises
rubrics_metrics.description: The deductions which Bacon abolished were from premises hastily snatched up, or arbitrarily assumed. The principles were neither established by legitimate canons of experimental inquiry, nor the results tested by that indispensable element of a rational Deductive Method, verification by specific experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not perform deduction from unverified or arbitrarily assumed premises. Deduction must be tied to premises established by legitimate experiment/observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of derivative laws into more general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative laws are such as are deducible from, and may ... be resolved into, other and more general ones. Many important scientific advances consist in resolving observed special laws into simpler, more general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess explanatory success by the degree to which a proposed law reduces or unifies previously separate empirical regularities (examples: atomic theory explaining chemical proportions; electricity explaining magnetism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between ultimate and derivative laws (limits of explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between two kinds of laws: ultimate laws, and derivative laws. Derivative laws are deducible from other and more general ones. Ultimate laws are those which cannot be so resolved. Ultimate laws cannot possibly be less numerous than the distinguishable sensations or other feelings of our nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of reduction: some aspects of experience (e.g., particular sensations like color) imply ultimate laws that cannot be wholly replaced by laws of a different kind. Be cautious of overreduction that ignores qualitatively distinct phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of hypotheses as provisional but subject to test
rubrics_metrics.description: These general truths will doubtless make their first appearance in the character of hypotheses; not proved, nor even admitting of proof, in the first instance, but assumed as premises for the purpose of deducing from them the known laws of concrete phenomena. But this, though their initial, cannot be their final state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hypotheses as starting points that must be submitted to induction/experiment. A hypothesis may be useful provisionally, but acceptance requires empirical testing and potential revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory theories should both justify old empiricisms and suggest improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical generalizations on which the operations of the arts have usually been founded, are continually justified and confirmed on the one hand, or corrected and improved on the other, by the discovery of the simpler scientific laws on which the efficacy of those operations depends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a theory by its capacity to explain prior empirical rules-of-thumb (e.g., agricultural rotation, manures) and to propose better, law-grounded practices in applied domains (medicine, agriculture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hypotheses to search for fresh instances and make predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature previously unknown has been brought to light... of examining all cases which present the conditions necessary for bringing that law into action; a process fertile in demonstrations of special laws previously unsuspected, and explanations of others already empirically known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good hypothesis or law directs attention to novel contexts where its conditions obtain (example: Faraday's law predicts electricity generation where conductor moves at right angles to magnetic direction). Use laws to generate testable predictions and to guide further observation/experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating hypotheses as final without empirical grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis being a mere supposition, there are no other limits to hypotheses than those of the human imagination; ... there is probably no hypothesis in the history of science in which both the agent itself and the law of its operation were fictitious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of hypotheses that are imaginative but lack empirical anchors; they may be heuristically useful, but should not be accepted as truths until tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation judged by capacity to reduce complexities and unify phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest achievements in physical science have consisted in resolving one observed law of the production of motion into the laws of other known modes of production, or the laws of several such modes into one more general mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanatory schemes that unify diverse phenomena under fewer, simpler principles (e.g., unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics under gravitation). Such unification is a key metric of explanatory power.
